implementation_notes: Ruby's Class#new is just allocate plus initialize, both overridable, so the creation owner is conventionally a class method - Order.from_cart(cart), Order.reconstitute(row) - that validates and calls new, with private_class_method :new as the (conventional, not enforced) way to make the factory the only door. Keyword arguments with required keywords make the constructor self-describing, Struct.new(..., keyword_init: true) provides a typed alternative constructor, and schema coercion libraries (dry-struct) take over raw-data conversion where the shape is complex. Validation belongs in initialize (guards that raise) or in the factory method, never in a caller-side check.
code_sketch:
class Order
  def self.from_cart(cart)
    raise ArgumentError, "empty cart" if cart.items.empty?
    new(id: OrderId.new, customer_id: cart.customer_id, items: cart.items)
  end
  def initialize(id:, customer_id:, items:)
    raise ArgumentError, "customer required" if customer_id.nil?
    @id, @customer_id, @items = id, customer_id, items.freeze
  end

  private_class_method :new   # convention: callers must use the factories
end
pitfalls: Ruby cannot truly hide construction: private_class_method :new stops new but not allocate/send, so treat the factory as a convention backed by validation, not as an enforced door.
initialize's return value is ignored; returning nil to signal failure silently produces a broken object - raise or use a class method that returns nil/explicit errors.
Required keyword gaps (id:) versus optional ones hide absent inputs, so validation based on nil checks alone misses fields that were never passed.
